help_feed_filter_intro.message: Feed filter consists of rules - one rule per line. Each rule defines a search string and a command, which must be performed if the search string matches. There are five kinds of rule-commands: Accept, Reject, Require, Options, Comment.

help_feed_filter_rule_def.description: Rule syntax definition. $1, $2 are <strong> tags for bold formatting.

help_feed_filter_cmd_a.message: A - declares Accept-rule. Rules are accept-rules by default, the "A:" can be omitted. If the feed item matches to the rule the item is considered good and no further rules are checked.
help_feed_filter_cmd_a.description: Command A description in filter help.

help_feed_filter_cmd_r.message: R - declares Reject-rule. If the feed item matches to the rule the item is considered bad and no further rules are checked.
help_feed_filter_cmd_r.description: Command R description in filter help.

help_feed_filter_cmd_q.message: Q - declares Require-rule. If the feed item DOES NOT match to the rule the item is considered bad and no further rules are checked.
help_feed_filter_cmd_q.description: Command Q description in filter help.

help_feed_filter_cmd_o.message: O - declares Options-rule. If the feed item matches to the rule the options declared in the rule are set for the item. The item is neither accepted nor rejected via this rule but can be accepted later by one of Accept-rules. In this case the item will have its options already set (unless the Accept-rule overrides them).
help_feed_filter_cmd_o.description: Command O description in filter help.

help_feed_filter_cmd_hash.message: # - lines starting with # are considered comments and are ignored. You can use comments to explain complex rules or to temporary disable rules for debugging.
help_feed_filter_cmd_hash.description: Comment (#) command description in filter help.

help_feed_filter_options_title.description: Options section title in filter help.

help_feed_filter_options_intro.message: Options allow to set properties on nzb-file. It's a comma-separated list of property names with their values. $1Definition of an option: name:value$2
help_feed_filter_options_intro.description: Options introduction text. $1, $2 are <strong> tags for bold formatting.

help_feed_filter_options_list.message: category (cat, c) - set category name, value is a string; pause (p) - add nzb in paused or unpaused state, possible values are: yes (y), no (n); priority (pr, r) - set priority, value is a signed integer number; priority+ (pr+, r+) - increase priority, value is a signed integer number; dupescore (ds, s) - set duplicate score, value is a signed integer number; dupescore+ (ds+, s+) - increase duplicate score, value is a signed integer number; dupekey (dk, k) - set duplicate key, value is a string; dupekey+ (dk+, k+) - add to duplicate key, value is a string; dupemode (dm, m) - set duplicate check mode, possible values are: score (s), all (a), force (f). For Score and All item is skipped if a duplicate marked as good exists in history; rageid - generate duplicate key using this rageid (integer number) and season/episode numbers; tvdbid - similar to rageid but uses tvdbid-field; tvmazeid - similar to rageid but uses tvmazeid-field; series - generate duplicate key using series identifier (any unique string) and season/episode numbers.
help_feed_filter_options_list.description: Options list table content in filter help.

help_feed_filter_options_override.message: Rule-options override values set in feed-options.

help_feed_filter_search_title.description: Search string section title in filter help.

help_feed_filter_search_intro.message: The search string is similar to used in search engines. It consists of search terms separated with spaces. Every term is checked for a feed item and if they all succeed the rule is considered matching. $1Definition of a term: [+|-][field:][command]param$2
help_feed_filter_search_intro.description: Search string introduction. $1, $2 are <strong> tags for bold formatting.

help_feed_filter_search_terms.message: + - declares a positive term. Terms are positive by default, the + can be omitted; - - declares a negative term. If the term succeeds the rule does not match; field - field to which apply the term. If not specified the default field title is used; command - a special character defining how to interpret the parameter; param - parameter for command.

help_feed_filter_search_commands.message: @ - search for string param. This is default command, the @ can be omitted; $ - param defines a regular expression (using POSIX Extended Regular Expressions syntax); = - equal; < - less than; <= - equal or less than; > - greater than; >= - equal or greater than.

help_feed_filter_text_fields.message: Commands @ and $ are for use with text fields (title, filename, category, link, description, dupekey, dupestatus).
help_feed_filter_text_fields.description: Info about text fields for search commands.

help_feed_filter_numeric_fields.message: Commands =, <, <=, > and >= are for use with numeric fields (size, age, imdbid, rageid, tvdbid, tvmazeid, season, episode, priority, dupescore).
help_feed_filter_numeric_fields.description: Info about numeric fields for search commands.

help_feed_filter_newznab.message: Any newznab attribute (encoded as newznab:attr in the RSS feed) can be used as search field with prefix attr-, for example attr-genre.

help_feed_filter_text_search_detailed.message: Text search supports wildcard characters * (matches any number of any characters), ? (matches any one character) and # (matches one digit). Text search is by default performed against words (word-search mode): the field content is separated into words and then each word is checked against pattern. If the search pattern starts and ends with * (star) the search is performed against the whole field content (substring-search mode). If the search pattern contains word separator characters (except * and ?) the search is performed on the whole field (the word-search would be obviously never successful in this case). Word separators: !$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~

help_feed_filter_numeric_detailed.message: Field size can have suffixes K or KB for kilobytes, M or MB for megabytes and G or GB for gigabytes. Field age can have suffixes m for minutes, h for hours and d for days. If suffix is not specified default is days.
help_feed_filter_numeric_detailed.description: Detailed info about numeric field suffixes.

help_feed_filter_fields_note.message: Only fields title, filename and age are always present. The availability of other fields depend on rss feed provider.

config_desc_maindir.message:
Root directory for all tasks.

On POSIX you can use "~" as alias for home directory (e.g. "~/downloads").
On Windows use absolute paths (e.g. "C:\Downloads").
config_desc_maindir.description: Description for the option MainDir DO NOT translate technical values enclosed in quotes.

config_desc_destdir.message:
Destination directory for downloaded files.

If you want to distinguish between partially downloaded files and
completed downloads, use also option <InterDir>.
config_desc_destdir.description: Description for the option DestDir DO NOT translate option names enclosed in angle brackets (e.g., <OptionName>).

config_desc_interdir.message:
Directory to store intermediate files.

If this option is set (not empty) the files are downloaded into
this directory first. After successful download of nzb-file (possibly
after par-repair) the files are moved to destination directory
(option <DestDir>). If download or unpack fail the files remain in
intermediate directory.

Using of intermediate directory can significantly improve unpack
performance if you can put intermediate directory (option <InterDir>)
and destination directory (option <DestDir>) on separate physical
hard drives.

NOTE: If the option <InterDir> is set to empty value the downloaded
files are put directly to destination directory (option <DestDir>).
config_desc_interdir.description: Description for the option InterDir DO NOT translate option names enclosed in angle brackets (e.g., <OptionName>). DO NOT translate the exact uppercase keywords (NOTE:, WARNING:, INFO:, INFO FOR DEVELOPERS:, MORE INFO:) as they are used to render UI badges.

config_desc_queuedir.message:
Directory to store program state.

This directory is used to save download queue, history, information
about fetched RSS feeds, statistics, etc.

config_desc_webdir.message:
Directory with web-interface files.

Example: /usr/local/share/nzbget/webui.

NOTE: To disable web-interface set the option to an empty value.
This however doesn't disable the built-in web-server completely because
it is also used to serve JSON-/XML-RPC requests.
config_desc_webdir.description: Description for the option WebDir DO NOT translate the exact uppercase keywords (NOTE:, WARNING:, INFO:, INFO FOR DEVELOPERS:, MORE INFO:) as they are used to render UI badges.

config_desc_scriptdir.message:
Directory with post-processing and other scripts.

This option may contain multiple directories separated with commas or semicolons.

NOTE: For information on writing scripts visit https://nzbget.com/documentation/extension-scripts/.
config_desc_scriptdir.description: Description for the option ScriptDir DO NOT translate the exact uppercase keywords (NOTE:, WARNING:, INFO:, INFO FOR DEVELOPERS:, MORE INFO:) as they are used to render UI badges.

config_desc_lockfile.message:
Lock-file for daemon-mode, POSIX only.

When started in daemon mode the program creates the lock file and
writes process-id (PID) into it. That info can be used in shell
scripts. If the lock file can not be created or the lock to the file
can not be acquired the daemon terminates, preventing unintentional
starting of multiple daemons.

Set to empty value to disable the creating of the lock-file and the
check for another running instance (not recommended).

config_desc_logfile.message:

config_desc_feed_filter.message:
Filter rules for items.

Use filter to ignore unwanted items in the feed. In its simplest version
the filter is a space separated list of words which must be present in
the item title.

Example: linux debian dvd.

MORE INFO:
NOTE: This is a short documentation, for more information visit
https://nzbget.com/documentation/rss/.

Feed filter consists of rules - one rule per line. Each rule defines
a search string and a command, which must be performed if the search
string matches. There are five kinds of rule-commands: Accept,
Reject, Require, Options, Comment.

NOTE: Since options in the configuration file can not span multiple
lines, the lines (rules) must be separated with %-character (percent).

Definition of a rule:
 [A:|A(options):|R:|Q:|O(options):|#] search-string

 A - declares Accept-rule. Rules are accept-rules by default, the
     "A:" can be omitted. If the feed item matches to the rule the
     item is considered good and no further rules are checked.
 R - declares Reject-rule. If the feed item matches to the rule the
     item is considered bad and no further rules are checked.
 Q - declares Require-rule. If the feed item DOES NOT match to the rule
     the item is considered bad and no further rules are checked.
 O - declares Options-rule. If the feed item matches to the rule the
     options declared in the rule are set for the item. The item is
     neither accepted nor rejected via this rule but can be accepted
     later by one of Accept-rules. In this case the item will have its
     options already set (unless the Accept-rule overrides them).
 # - lines starting with # are considered comments and are ignored. You
     can use comments to explain complex rules or to temporary disable
     rules for debugging.

Options allow to set properties on nzb-file. It's a comma-separated
list of property names with their values.

Definition of an option:
 name:value

Options can be defined using long option names or short names:
 category (cat, c)    - set category name, value is a string;
 pause (p)            - add nzb in paused or unpaused state, possible
                        values are: yes (y), no (n);
 priority (pr, r)     - set priority, value is a signed integer number;
 priority+ (pr+, r+)  - increase priority, value is a signed integer number;
 dupescore (ds, s)    - set duplicate score, value is a signed integer number;
 dupescore+ (ds+, s+) - increase duplicate score, value is a signed integer number;
 dupekey (dk, k)      - set duplicate key, value is a string;
 dupekey+ (dk+, k+)   - add to duplicate key, value is a string;
 dupemode (dm, m)     - set duplicate check mode, possible values
                        are: score (s), all (a), force (f);
 rageid				- generate duplicate key using this rageid
                        (integer number) and season/episode numbers;
 series				- generate duplicate key using series identifier
                        (any unique string) and season/episode numbers.

Examples of option definitions:
 Accept(category:my series, pause:yes, priority:100): my show 1080p;
 Options(c:my series, p:y, r:100): 1080p;
 Options(s:1000): 1080p;
 Options(k+:1080p): 1080p;
 Options(dupemode:force): BluRay.

Rule-options override values set in feed-options.

The search-string is similar to used in search engines. It consists of
search terms separated with spaces. Every term is checked for a feed
item and if they all succeed the rule is considered matching.

Definition of a term:
 [+|-][field:][command]param

 +       - declares a positive term. Terms are positive by default,
           the "+" can be omitted;
 -       - declares a negative term. If the term succeeds the feed
           item is ignored;
 field   - field to which apply the term. If not specified
           the default field "title" is used;
 command - a special character defining how to interpret the
           parameter (followed after the command):
           @  - search for string "param". This is default command,
                the "@" can be omitted;
           $  - "param" defines a regular expression (using POSIX Extended
                Regular Expressions syntax);
           =  - equal;
           <  - less than;
           <= - equal or less than;
           >  - greater than;
           >= - equal or greater than;
 param   - parameter for command.

Commands @ and $ are for use with text fields (title, filename, category,
link, description, dupekey). Commands =, <, <=, > and >= are for use
with numeric fields (size, age, imdbid, rageid, season, episode, priority,
dupescore).

Only fields title, filename and age are always present. The availability of
other fields depend on rss feed provider.

Any newznab attribute (encoded as "newznab:attr" in the RSS feed) can
be used as search field with prefix "attr-", for example "attr-genre".

Text search (Command @) supports wildcard characters * (matches
any number of any characters), ? (matches any one character)
and # (matches one digit).
Text search is by default performed against words (word-search mode): the
field content is separated into words and then each word is checked
against pattern. If the search pattern starts and ends with * (star)
the search is performed against the whole field content
(substring-search mode). If the search pattern contains word separator
characters (except * and ?) the search is performed on the whole
field (the word-search would be obviously never successful in this
case). Word separators are: !\"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\\]^_`{|}~.

Field "size" can have suffixes "K" or "KB" for kilobytes, "M" or "MB"
for megabytes and "G" or "GB" for gigabytes. Field "age" can have
suffixes "m" for minutes, "h" for hours and "d" for days. If suffix
is not specified default is days.

Examples (the trailing ; or . is not part of filter):
1) A: s01* -category:anime;
2) my show WEB-DL;
3) *my?show* WEB-DL size:<1.8GB age:>2h;
4) R: size:>9GB;
5) Q: HDTV.

NOTE: This is a short documentation, for more information visit
https://nzbget.com/documentation/rss/.

same. Duplicate keys are set by fetching from RSS feeds using title
identifier fields provided by RSS provider (imdbid or rageid/season/episode).

If duplicates were detected only one of them is downloaded. If download
fails another duplicate is tried. If download succeeds all remaining
duplicates are deleted from queue.

NOTE: For automatic duplicate handling option <HealthCheck> must be
set to "Delete", "Park" or "None". If it is set to "Pause" you will need to
manually unpause another duplicate (if any exists in queue).

NOTE: For more info on duplicates see https://nzbget.com/documentation/rss/.

config_desc_dupearticlefallback.message:
Fetch missing articles from duplicate collections.

When an article cannot be downloaded from any news server, the program
looks for duplicates of the collection (same title or duplicate key, see
option <DupeCheck>) in download queue and history and retries the article
using the message-id of the equivalent article of the duplicate. This can
rescue downloads where each posting of the same content is incomplete on
its own but the postings complete each other.

Value "article" borrows articles only from files which match the failed
file exactly in article count and closely in size; borrowed articles
declaring a different file size are discarded. Small mismatches at
segment boundaries can remain and are repaired by par-check. Value "yes"
is accepted as an alias for "article" for compatibility with older
versions.

When the primary posting proves to be missing many articles of a file,
the remaining articles of that file are requested from the duplicate
first (with the primary kept as a final fallback), instead of paying
a failing sweep over all news servers per article. Independently, the
duplicate that is tried first is not fixed: whenever it misses several
articles in a row, the next duplicate (in duplicate-score order) takes
its place, so one badly holed posting does not slow down recovery when
other duplicates could serve the articles. All duplicates and the
primary remain fetch sources for every article regardless of which one
is tried first.

Value "stream" additionally repairs files on byte level after download:
byte ranges which no news server could supply are fetched from a
duplicate posting that carries the same bytes, even when that posting
was split into articles differently. This recovers reposts of ANY
release - password-protected and compressed archives and their par2
files included, since the repair copies posted bytes without ever
unpacking or decrypting them.
It also recovers across DIFFERENT packagings of the same inner media
file, as long as the content bytes were not transformed: a directly
posted file, store-mode (uncompressed) rar volumes, stored zip (also
spanned), 7-Zip in copy mode (also .001 splits) and raw file splits
can all donate to each other, even when volume sizes differ.
Compressed archives can only donate to byte-identical reposts of
themselves: bridging two different compression runs is physically
impossible.
With option <DupeStreamDecompress> enabled and an extractor configured,
byte-level repair also bridges DIFFERENT compressions of the same inner
media file by decompressing the donor first; without it, two different
compression runs still cannot donate to each other directly.
Password-protected store-mode rar archives (rar3 and rar5) are mapped
and cross-packed the same way as unencrypted ones when nzbget knows the
archive's password - supplied via the NZB's password field, not typed
in here - including bridging two DIFFERENT passwords on either side of
a repair. Without a known password an encrypted archive can still only
donate to a byte-identical repost of itself.
Content identity is verified against already downloaded bytes before
anything is written; par-check remains active as final verification.
The damaged download must survive until post-processing for the repair
to run (option <HealthCheck> values "delete" and "park" can remove it
before that).

Value "live" includes everything "stream" does and additionally runs
the byte-level repair DURING download: as soon as a damaged file of the
collection completes (while its other files are still downloading), the
missing byte ranges are fetched from the duplicates right away instead
of waiting for the whole download to finish. Each damaged file gets one
such early attempt (without the decompression step of option
<DupeStreamDecompress>); post-processing remains the final authority -
it retries whatever is left, applies the health accounting below and
hands over to par-check as usual.

NOTE: Health statistics are recounted for the bytes stream repair
recovers. A file is credited back to health only once ALL of its holes
are filled, so a release whose files are therefore fully repaired
reaches full health and completes normally (moved to its destination
directory) even without par-files. A release that is only partially
repaired is credited nothing for its still-damaged files, so it keeps
its failed status and its files remain in the intermediate directory;
with par-files present the requested par-check verifies the repaired
file and the download completes normally.

Duplicates whose packaging stream repair cannot cross-map (e.g.
compressed archives, an encrypted archive whose password is unknown, or
an unrelated inner file) cannot be merged this way; for these cases
duplicate handling (option <DupeCheck>) and par-repair using files of
duplicates (option <ParScan=dupe>) remain in effect.

NOTE: The source nzb-files of duplicates must still exist in directory
<NzbDir> (option <NzbCleanupDisk> must be disabled) for articles to be
borrowed from history items.

config_desc_dupestreamdecompress.message:
Recover byte-identical content from compressed duplicate archives.

Option <DupeArticleFallback> value "stream" only donates bytes that are
copyable without decompression (store-mode rar/zip/7z, raw splits, directly
posted media). A duplicate posted as a normally-compressed archive (deflate
zip, LZMA 7z, compressed rar) of the same inner media file cannot donate
under that scheme, because its posted bytes are a compression of the
content, not the content itself.

When this option is enabled and "stream" repair still has holes after
trying every store-mode/split/bare donor, nzbget materializes a compressed
duplicate's member files to a temporary directory and runs the configured
extractor (<UnrarCmd>/<SevenZipCmd>) on them to recover the inner file's
plaintext bytes, which are then verified and patched exactly like any other
stream-repair donor.

This is an opt-in, heavier last resort: it fetches and decompresses an
entire duplicate archive (bounded by an internal size cap) instead of only
the byte ranges needed, and requires a working extractor. It only helps a
target that "stream" can otherwise map to its inner content (directly
posted media, or store/copy-mode rar/zip/7z/split archives with holes); a
compressed target still cannot be repaired this way, since there is no
plaintext location to write into a compressed member.

Memory limit for article cache.

If option <DirectWrite> is disabled the cache should be big enough to
hold all articles of one file (typically up to 200 MB, sometimes even
500 MB). Otherwise the articles are written into temporary directory
when the cache is full, which degrades performance.

Value "0" disables article cache.

In 32 bit mode the maximum allowed value is 1900.

config_desc_directwrite.message:
Write decoded articles directly into destination output file.

Files are posted to Usenet in multiple pieces (articles). Each file
typically consists of hundreds of articles.

When option <DirectWrite> is disabled and the article cache (option
<ArticleCache>) is not active or is full the program saves downloaded
articles into temporary directory and later reads them all to write
again into the destination file.

When option <DirectWrite> is enabled the program at first creates the
output destination file with required size (total size of all articles),
then writes the articles directly to this file without creating of any
temporary files. If article cache (option <ArticleCache>) is active
the downloaded articles are saved into cache first and are written
into the destination file when the cache flushes. This happen when
all articles of the file are downloaded or when the cache becomes
full to 90%.

The direct write relies on the ability of file system to create
empty files without allocating the space on the drive (sparse files),
which most modern file systems support including EXT3, EXT4
and NTFS. The notable exception is HFS+ (default file system on OSX).

The direct write usually improves performance by reducing the amount
of disk operations but may produce more fragmented files when used
without article cache.

config_desc_writebuffer.message:
Memory limit for per connection write buffer.

When downloaded articles are written into disk the OS collects
data in the internal buffer before flushing it into disk. This option
controls the size of this buffer per connection/download thread.

Larger buffers decrease the amount of disk operations and help
producing less fragmented files speeding up the post-processing
(unpack).

To calculate the maximum memory required for all download threads multiply
WriteBuffer by number of connections configured in section
"NEWS-SERVERS". The option sets the limit, the actual buffer can be
smaller if the article size (typically about 500 KB) is below the limit.

Write-buffer is managed by OS (system libraries) and therefore
the effect of the option is highly OS-dependent.

Recommended value for computers with enough memory: 1024.

Value "0" disables the setting of buffer size. In this case a buffer
of default size (OS and compiler specific) is used, which is usually
too small (1-4 KB) and therefore not optimal.

NOTE: Also see option <ArticleCache>.

config_desc_poststrategy.message:

              task from running even if the item does not require a par repair;
 Balanced   - items that do not need par repair are post processed one at a
              time while par repair tasks may also run simultaneously one after
              another at the same time. This means that a post process par
              repair will not prevent another task from running, but at a cost
              of using more computer resource;
 Aggressive - will simultaneously post process up to three items including
              one par repair task;
 Rocket     - will simultaneously post process up to six items including one
              or two par repair tasks.

NOTE: Computer resources are in heavy demand when post-processing with
simultaneous tasks - make sure the hardware is capable.
